data.description: Machine-readable TypeScript code style rules extracted from Google TypeScript Style Guide. Each item is one rule with RFC 2119 severity, trigger, one-sentence rule, optional example, and source anchor.

severityLegend.MUST: Absolute requirement (RFC 2119). Imperative/declarative statements also map to MUST.
severityLegend.SHOULD: Strong recommendation; valid reasons may exist to ignore (RFC 2119). Maps to 'prefer'.
severityLegend.SHOULD_NOT: Strong recommendation against; valid reasons may exist to ignore (RFC 2119). Maps to 'avoid'.

items.rule: Source files are encoded in UTF-8.
Use only ASCII horizontal space character for whitespace in source files.
Use special escape sequences for characters that have them.
Never use legacy octal escapes.
Use actual Unicode character for non-ASCII printable characters.
Files consist of copyright, @fileoverview, imports, implementation in order.
Separate each file section with exactly one blank line.
Add license or copyright information in a JSDoc at the top of the file.
Do not indent wrapped lines in @fileoverview JSDoc.
TypeScript code must use paths to import other TypeScript code.
Import paths may be relative or rooted at base directory.
Use relative imports when referring to files within same project.
Prefer named imports for symbols used frequently or with clear names.
Prefer namespace imports when using many symbols from large APIs.
Fix name collisions by using namespace import or renaming exports.
Rename imports if needed to avoid collisions or improve clarity.
Use import type when imported symbol is only used as a type.
Code must refer to code in other files using ES6 imports and exports.
Code must not use the namespace Foo construct.
Namespaces may only be used when required by external third-party code.
Code must not use require for imports.
Use named exports in all code.
Do not use default exports.
Only export symbols that are used outside of the module.
Minimize the exported API surface of modules.
Do not use export let for mutable exports.
Use explicit getter functions for externally accessible mutable bindings.
Do not create container classes with static methods for namespacing.
Use export type when re-exporting a type.
Use const for variables that never change and let for variables that do.
Do not use var for variable declarations.
Variables must not be used before their declaration.
Every local variable declaration declares only one variable.
Do not use the Array constructor with or without new.
Use bracket notation or Array.from to initialize arrays.
Do not define or use non-numeric properties on arrays.
When creating an array only spread iterables.
Primitives including null and undefined must not be spread into arrays.
Specify [] as default value for optional destructured array parameters.
Provide default values on left hand side of destructured parameters.
Prefer object destructuring to array destructuring when possible.
The Object constructor is disallowed.
Use object literal instead of Object constructor.
Do not use unfiltered for in statements.
Filter for-in loops explicitly or use for of with Object.keys.
When creating an object only objects may be spread.
Arrays and primitives must not be spread into objects.
Avoid spreading objects with prototypes other than Object prototype.
Computed non-symbol property names must not be mixed with non-quoted keys.
Deeper levels of nesting may not be used in parameter destructuring.
Computed properties may not be used in parameter destructuring.
Specify default values in left-hand-side of destructured parameter.
Optional destructured object parameter must default to {}.
Class declarations must not be terminated with semicolons.
Statements containing class expressions must be terminated with semicolon.
Class method declarations must not use semicolons.
Method declarations should be separated by single blank line.
The toString method may be overridden.
toString must always succeed and never have visible side effects.
Prefer module-local functions over private static methods.
Code should not rely on dynamic dispatch of static methods.
Static methods should only be called on the base class itself.
Static methods should not be called on variables containing dynamic instance.
Static methods must not be called on subclass that does not define method.
Code must not use this in a static context.
Constructor calls must use parentheses even with no arguments.
Constructors with parameter properties should not be omitted.
Constructor should be separated by single blank line above and below.
Do not use private fields also known as private identifiers.
Use TypeScript visibility annotations instead of private identifiers.
Mark properties never reassigned outside constructor with readonly modifier.
Use TypeScript parameter property for obvious initializers.
Initialize class member where declared if not a parameter.
Properties used outside class lexical scope must not use private visibility.
TypeScript code must not use obj[foo] to bypass property visibility.
Getters and setters for class members may be used.
Getter method must be a pure function with no side effects.
Getters must not change observable state.
At least one accessor for a property must be non-trivial.
Getters and setters must not be defined using Object.defineProperty.
Computed properties may only be used in classes when property is symbol.
Dict-style properties are not allowed in classes.
Define Symbol.iterator method for classes that are logically iterable.
Limit symbol visibility as much as possible.
Never use public modifier except for non-readonly public parameter properties.
Do not manipulate prototypes directly in ordinary implementation code.
Modifying prototypes of builtin objects is explicitly forbidden.
Prefer function declarations over arrow functions or function expressions.
Arrow functions may be used when explicit type annotation is required.
Nested functions may use function declarations or arrow functions.
Arrow functions are preferred in method bodies for outer this access.
Do not use function expressions.
Use arrow functions instead of function expressions.
Function expressions may be used only for dynamic this rebinding.
Function expressions may be used for generator functions.
Only use concise body if return value is actually used.
Use block body when return value of function is not used.
Do not pass built-in functions that take more than one argument as callbacks.
Prefer passing arrow function that explicitly forwards parameters.
Classes usually should not contain properties initialized to arrow functions.
Always use arrow functions to call instance methods.
Do not obtain or pass references to instance methods.
Event handlers may use arrow functions when no need to uninstall.
Arrow function properties are right approach when uninstallation required.
Do not use bind in expression that installs event handler.
Optional function parameters may be given default initializer.
Initializers must not have observable side effects.
Initializers should be kept as simple as possible.
Prefer destructuring when many optional parameters without natural order.
Use rest parameter instead of accessing arguments.
Never name local variable or parameter arguments.
Use function spread syntax instead of Function.prototype.apply.
Blank lines at start or end of function body are not allowed.
Single blank line may be used within function bodies for logical groupings.
Attach * to function and yield keywords.
Do not put space after ... in rest or spread syntax.
Only use this in class constructors and methods.
Only use this in functions with explicit this type declared.
Only use this in arrow functions defined in scope where this may be used.
Never use this to refer to global object.
Never use this to refer to context of eval.
Never use this to refer to target of event.
Never use this for unnecessarily called or applied functions.
Control flow statements always use braced blocks for containing code.
First statement of non-empty block must begin on its own line.
If statements fitting on one line may elide the block.
Prefer to avoid assignment of variables inside control statements.
Enclose assignment in additional parenthesis when preferred.
Prefer for of someArr to iterate over arrays.
Array.prototype.forEach and vanilla for loops are also allowed.
For-in loops may only be used on dict-style objects.
Do not use for in to iterate over arrays.
Use Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty in for-in loops.
Prefer for-of with Object keys values entries over for-in.
Do not use unnecessary parentheses around expression following keywords.
Always use new Error when instantiating exceptions.
Only throw Error types or their subtypes.
When catching errors assume all thrown errors are instances of Error.
Exception handlers must not defensively handle non-Error types.
Explain reason for empty catch block in comment.
All switch statements must contain default statement group.
Default statement group must be last.
Non-empty statement groups must not fall through.
Empty statement groups are allowed to fall through.
Always use triple equals and not equals.
Comparisons to literal null may use == and != operators.
Do not use type and non-nullability assertions without reason.
Explicitly write runtime check to assert type or non-nullability.
Add clarification to explain why unsafe assertion is OK.
Comments may not be necessary if reasoning is obvious.
Type assertions must use the as syntax.
Use unknown as intermediate type for double assertions.
Use type annotations instead of type assertions for object literals.
Limit amount of code inside try block without hurting readability.
Widening try blocks to cover whole loop is ok for performance.
Do not define new decorators.
Only use decorators defined by frameworks.
Decorator must immediately precede symbol with no empty lines.
TypeScript code must not instantiate wrapper classes for primitives.
Do not rely on Automatic Semicolon Insertion.
Explicitly end all statements using semicolon.
Code must not use const enum.
Debugger statements must not be included in production code.
Do not use the with keyword.
Do not use eval or Function constructor except for code loaders.
Do not use non-standard ECMAScript or Web Platform features.
Do not use features marked deprecated or removed from ECMAScript.
Do not use ECMAScript features not yet standardized.
Do not use proposed but not-yet-complete web standards.
Do not use non-standard language extensions.
Never modify builtin types by adding methods to constructors or prototypes.
Avoid depending on libraries that modify builtin types.
Do not add symbols to global object unless absolutely necessary.
Identifiers must use only ASCII letters digits underscores and rarely $.
Names should not be decorated with information included in type.
Do not use trailing or leading underscores for private properties.
Do not use opt_ prefix for optional parameters.
Suffixing Observables with $ should be consistent within projects.
Names must be descriptive and clear to new reader.
Do not use abbreviations ambiguous or unfamiliar to readers outside project.
Treat abbreviations like acronyms as whole words, use loadHttpUrl not loadHTTPUrl.
Identifiers should not generally use $ except when required by third-party frameworks.
Type parameters may use a single upper case character T or UpperCamelCase.
Test method names in xUnit frameworks may use _ separators like testX_whenY_doesZ().
Identifiers must not use _ as a prefix or suffix, including _ by itself.
Module namespace imports must use lowerCamelCase while files are snake_case.
CONSTANT_CASE indicates a value is intended not to be changed, may be used for technically mutable values.
Values that can be instantiated more than once must use lowerCamelCase, not CONSTANT_CASE.
Local aliases must match the existing naming and format of the source identifier.
Code may rely on type inference for all type expressions including variables, fields, return types.
Leave out type annotations for trivially inferred types like string, number, boolean, RegExp literals.
Explicitly specify types for empty generic types to prevent inference as unknown.
Whether to include return type annotations is up to the code author, not a general requirement.
Type aliases must not include |null or |undefined, only add when the alias is actually used.
Use optional fields and parameters with ? rather than a |undefined type.

good: interface CoffeeOrder { sugarCubes: number; milk?: Whole|LowFat|HalfHalf; }

items.rule: When providing a structural implementation, explicitly include the type at the declaration.
Use interfaces to define structural types for objects, not classes or type aliases.

good: interface User { firstName: string; lastName: string; }
bad: type User = { firstName: string, lastName: string }

items.rule: When declaring types for objects, use interfaces instead of type alias for object literal.

good: interface User { firstName: string; lastName: string; }
bad: type User = { firstName: string, lastName: string }

items.rule: For simple types use T[] or readonly T[] rather than Array<T> or ReadonlyArray<T>.
For complex types use the longer form Array<T> instead of syntax sugar.

good: let e: Array<{n: number, s: string}>;

items.rule: Provide a meaningful label for the key in index signatures, not just 'key'.
Always use the simplest type construct, a little repetition is cheaper than complex types.
Consider not using any, prefer providing a more specific type, using unknown, or documenting why.
Use unknown instead of any when you need to express that a type is unknown for safety.
Should not use {} for most use cases, prefer unknown, Record<string, T>, or object.
If creating a Pair type, use a tuple type instead of an interface.

bad: interface Pair { first: string; second: string; }

items.rule: Never use String, Boolean, Number wrapper types, always use lowercase primitives.
Never invoke wrapper types as constructors with new.
Avoid creating APIs with return type only generics, always specify generics explicitly when using them.
Do not use @ts-ignore, @ts-expect-error, or @ts-nocheck comments.
Use JSDoc for documentation comments users should read, use // for implementation comments.
Multi-line comments must use multiple single-line comments // not block comment style /* */.
Comments are not enclosed in boxes drawn with asterisks or other characters.
Single-line JSDoc overflowing to multiple lines must use multi-line style with /** and */ on own lines.

good: * Multiple lines of JSDoc text are written here,

items.rule: JSDoc comments must be well-formed as tools extract metadata for validation and optimization.
JSDoc is written in Markdown, use Markdown lists instead of plain text indentation.

good: * Computes weight based on three factors:
bad: * Computes weight based on three factors:

items.rule: Most JSDoc tags must occupy their own line with the tag at the beginning of the line.
Line-wrapped block tags are indented four spaces, horizontal alignment of description is discouraged.

good: @param foo This is a param with a particularly long description that just

items.rule: Do not indent when wrapping a @desc or @fileoverview description.
Document all top-level exports of modules with JSDoc comments, except tooling-only symbols.
Class JSDoc should provide enough information to know how and when to use the class.
Method, parameter, and return descriptions may be omitted if obvious from JSDoc or signature.
Method descriptions begin with a verb phrase in third person, not imperative sentence.
Document parameter properties using JSDoc @param annotation, not separate field comments.

good: * @param percolator The percolator used for brewing.

items.rule: Do not declare types in @param or @return blocks or write @implements, @enum, @private in TypeScript.
Avoid comments that just restate the parameter name and type without adding information.

bad: /** @param fooBarService The Bar service for the Foo application. */

items.rule: @param and @return lines may be omitted when they don't add information beyond the name and type.
Use parameter name comments when method name and value don't convey meaning, place before value with =.
Existing code may use legacy parameter name comment style after the value without = for consistency.
Write JSDoc before decorators like @Component, not between decorator and decorated statement.
Brand new files must use Google Style regardless of style choices of other files in the package.
When adding new code to a file not in Google Style, reformatting existing code first is recommended.
New code must not violate the style guide even when adding to non-style files.
It is not required to change all existing code to meet current style guidelines.
Be careful not to allow opportunistic style fixes to muddle the focus of a change list.
Mark deprecated methods, classes or interfaces with @deprecated JSDoc annotation including fix directions.
Source code generated by build process is not required to be in Google Style.
Generated identifiers referenced from hand-written code must follow naming requirements.
Generated identifiers may contain underscores as a special exception to avoid conflicts.
